cloze.text: The BLS sequence is {{c1::C-A-B}}: Circulation (cardiac compression), Airway (clear airway), Breathing (rescue breaths).
BLS step 1 — check responsiveness: tap and shout "Are you okay?" If no response, {{c1::call 911}} and send a second rescuer to retrieve the {{c2::AED}}.
When checking for a pulse in BLS, use the {{c1::carotid}} artery in adults and children and the {{c2::brachial}} artery in infants.
BLS: breathing normal AND pulse present → {{c1::monitor the patient until emergency help arrives}}.
BLS: pulse present but no normal breathing → give {{c1::rescue breathing only}}: adults 1 breath every {{c2::5–6 seconds}}; children/infants 1 breath every {{c3::3–5 seconds}}.
cloze.extra: The AHA flowchart on the page puts it as 1 breath every 6 seconds = 10 breaths/min for adults.

cloze.text: During rescue breathing, reassess the pulse every {{c1::2 minutes}}; if there is no pulse, start CPR. Use a {{c2::pocket mask or bag-valve mask}} if available.
If a patient receiving rescue breathing may have an opioid overdose, give {{c1::naloxone}}.
BLS: no pulse and no breathing (or only gasping) → {{c1::begin CPR immediately (30 compressions : 2 breaths)}} and use the AED as soon as possible.
AED rhythm check: if the rhythm is shockable, give {{c1::1 shock}}, then resume CPR for {{c2::2 minutes}} until the AED prompts another rhythm check. If not shockable, resume CPR for 2 minutes.
For chest compressions, place the hands on the {{c1::lower half of the sternum}}.
CPR compression depth: adults {{c1::at least 2 inches}}; children {{c2::about 2 inches (1/3 to 1/2 of chest depth)}}; infants {{c3::about 1.5 inches}}.
Infant compressions use {{c1::2 fingers}} for a single rescuer or {{c2::2 thumbs}} with 2 rescuers.
Compression-to-ventilation ratio: adults {{c1::30:2}} (1 or 2 rescuers); children/infants 30:2 with 1 rescuer and {{c2::15:2}} with 2 rescuers.
During CPR, let the chest {{c1::fully recoil}} between compressions, and keep interruptions to less than {{c2::10 seconds}} when switching or checking.
Before using the AED, make sure the patient is on a {{c1::firm, dry}} surface (use a board if needed), then expose the chest and {{c2::remove moisture}} before attaching the pads.
After the AED delivers a shock, {{c1::immediately resume CPR}}; if no shock is advised, resume CPR without delay.
Do not touch the patient while the AED is {{c1::analyzing or shocking}}.
Use the recovery position only if the patient is {{c1::unconscious but has a pulse and is breathing}}; turn the patient onto their {{c2::side}} to protect the airway and monitor until EMS arrives.
Normal adult body temperature is {{c1::97–99°F (36–37°C)}}; the most common temperature is {{c2::98.6°F}}.
A temperature above {{c1::99.6°F (37.6°C)}} indicates {{c2::pyrexia (fever)}}.
Normal respiratory rate: adult {{c1::12–20}} breaths per minute; child {{c2::18–22}} breaths per minute.
cloze.extra: Count respirations by watching the chest rise and fall.

cloze.text: Besides the rate, monitor the quality of the breath: its {{c1::sound, depth, and rhythm}}.
Normal resting heart rate: adult {{c1::60–100}} bpm; child {{c2::80–120}} bpm; infant {{c3::100–160}} bpm.
{{c1::β-blockers}}, resting and fasting can slow the heart rate; {{c2::exercise, stress and drugs}} can elevate it.
When taking a pulse, record beats per minute, {{c1::quality (weak or strong)}}, and {{c2::rhythm (regular or irregular)}}.

Pulse locations: radial artery — {{c1::lateral and ventral wrist}}; brachial — {{c2::medial aspect of the antecubital fossa}}; carotid — {{c3::lateral to the sternocleidomastoid}}; femoral — {{c4::medial aspect of the upper thigh}}.
In an emergency, the {{c1::carotid}} is the best artery for assessing the pulse.
If no pulse can be palpated after 10 seconds, assume {{c1::cardiac arrest}} and begin chest compressions at 100–120 per minute.
{{c1::Systolic}} BP is the force exerted during ventricular contraction; {{c2::diastolic}} BP is the resting pressure during ventricular relaxation.
{{c1::Korotkoff sounds}} are the sounds made by the vibrations of an artery under pressure.
The {{c1::sphygmomanometer}} measures blood pressure and the {{c2::stethoscope}} lets you hear blood passing through the arteries. Automated devices are {{c3::less accurate}} than the standard cuff.
Manual BP: inflate the cuff until the pulse disappears, then inflate another {{c1::20–30 mmHg}}; deflate slowly at {{c2::2–3 mmHg per second}}.
Manual BP: the pressure at which the pulse reappears is the {{c1::systolic}} pressure; the last sound before silence is the {{c2::diastolic}} pressure.

Hypertension is blood pressure elevated against the artery walls, often {{c1::with no symptoms}}; it can silently damage the heart, vessels, brain, and kidneys — so {{c2::early detection}} is critical.
cloze.extra: Did you know: almost 1 in 2 U.S. adults (about 1 in 4 in Canada) have high blood pressure, many without knowing it — the "silent killer".

cloze.text: Orthostatic hypotension = a drop of ≥{{c1::20}} mmHg systolic or ≥{{c2::10}} mmHg diastolic from supine to standing.
Causes of hypertension: chronic disease, stress, obesity, {{c1::salt intake}}, {{c2::kidney dysfunction}}, smoking.
Causes of orthostatic hypotension: prolonged chair time, standing too quickly, {{c1::dehydration}}, {{c2::antihypertensive medications}}.
If BP is extremely high and the patient shows signs (headache, vision issues, chest pain): {{c1::stop treatment}}, and {{c2::call 911}} if unstable.
Dizzy or fainting from hypotension: return the patient to the {{c1::supine position with feet slightly elevated}}, monitor vitals, raise slowly, and give oxygen if needed.
Hypertensive dental patients have an increased risk of {{c1::stroke or heart attack}} during procedures, especially under stress or with {{c2::vasoconstrictors}}.
Hypotensive dental patients risk {{c1::falls and fainting}} after sitting up or standing suddenly, especially after treatment.
Antihypertensives increase the risk of {{c1::hypotension}}, so schedule appointments {{c2::30–60 minutes}} after medications and meals.
To avoid orthostatic hypotension, let patients remain seated for {{c1::1–2 minutes}} before standing.

cloze.section: Hypertension and dental process of care
cloze.text: BP <140/<90: {{c1::proceed with routine care}} (healthy or well-controlled).
cloze.extra: Exam standard (AHA 2017): normal <120/<80; elevated 120–129/<80; stage 1 130–139 or 80–89; stage 2 ≥140 or ≥90; hypertensive crisis >180 and/or >120. The book's 'mild/moderate' wording is older terminology — the dental-management thresholds themselves are the book's.

cloze.section: Hypertension and dental process of care
cloze.text: BP 140–159/90–99: proceed with care and {{c1::monitor BP at each visit}} — minimal risk, but may worsen over time.

cloze.section: Hypertension and dental process of care
cloze.text: BP 160–179/100–109: proceed with caution — {{c1::recheck BP after 5 minutes}}, use stress reduction, consider a {{c2::medical consult}}.

cloze.section: Hypertension and dental process of care
cloze.text: BP ≥180/≥110 (even once): {{c1::stop elective care}}; recheck in 5 minutes, and if still elevated {{c2::refer for medical evaluation}} before treatment.
cloze.extra: Danger zone: high risk for stroke or MI.

cloze.section: Hypertension and dental process of care
cloze.text: Any BP + symptoms (headache, dizziness, chest pain): {{c1::stop immediately}}, regardless of the reading, and refer to emergency care or a physician — possible {{c2::hypertensive crisis or cardiac issue}}.

cloze.section: Hypertension and dental process of care
cloze.text: If a patient reports not taking (or missing) a dose of BP medication: ask {{c1::when they last took it}}, consider rechecking BP, and delay care if pressure is high.
cloze.extra: Skipped doses = uncontrolled pressure, which may cause treatment complications.

cloze.text: Syncope is caused by a drop in blood pressure, e.g. from {{c1::anxiety}}, dehydration, standing too quickly, or postural changes.
Seizure causes: {{c1::epilepsy}}, head trauma, brain infection, fever, drug reactions, low oxygen, or unknown triggers.
Early signs of syncope: warmth, nausea, lightheadedness, vision changes, {{c1::pale skin}}, and {{c2::sweating}}.
Early signs of a seizure: an {{c1::aura}} (odd sensation), staring, confusion, jerking of limbs.
During syncope: brief loss of consciousness (usually less than {{c1::5 minutes}}), limp body, fast recovery.
During a seizure: rhythmic muscle contractions, stiffness, may fall or lose consciousness, possible {{c1::incontinence}}.
Syncope: place the patient supine with legs slightly elevated — the {{c1::Trendelenburg position}}.
If recovery from syncope is delayed, use an {{c1::ammonia capsule}} under the nose.
Seizure: protect the patient from injury (clear surroundings, cushion head); do NOT {{c1::restrain the patient or place anything in the mouth}}.
Let a seizure run its course; call EMS if it lasts more than {{c1::5 minutes}} or if {{c2::another begins immediately after}}.
After a seizure ends, place the patient in the {{c1::recovery position (on their side)}}; monitor vitals and reassure.
Dental settings typically use a {{c1::modified Trendelenburg}} position — only the legs elevated, not full inversion.
A {{c1::TIA (transient ischemic attack)}}, or "mini-stroke", is a temporary blockage in the brain whose symptoms resolve within {{c2::24 hours}}; it is a warning sign of a future full stroke.
Most strokes are {{c1::ischemic}} (a clot blocks a cerebral artery); fewer are {{c2::hemorrhagic}} (a vessel bursts and bleeds into the brain).
Stroke contributors: {{c1::high blood pressure}}, {{c2::atherosclerosis}}, heart disease, smoking, diabetes, obesity, high cholesterol, and age.
cloze.extra: Board Alert: why medical history matters — a patient with high BP, heart disease or high cholesterol is at greater risk of a stroke or cardiac event during treatment. Boards test these links in case studies.

cloze.text: Besides F.A.S.T. (arm = numb or can't raise one arm; speech = slurred, confused), stroke signs include sudden confusion, vision changes, dizziness, {{c1::severe headache}}, or {{c2::one-sided numbness}}.
Stroke protocol: call 911 right away and note the {{c1::exact time symptoms began}} — hospital treatment is time-sensitive. Monitor vitals until EMS arrives.
Suspected stroke: give nothing by mouth (no food, water or medications); do NOT give {{c1::aspirin}} — it may be dangerous if the stroke is {{c2::hemorrhagic}}.
A mild allergic reaction is a localized immune reaction with {{c1::gradual}} onset — over several minutes to hours after exposure.
Anaphylaxis onset is {{c1::rapid — usually within seconds or minutes}} of exposure to the allergen.
Signs of a mild allergic reaction: erythema (redness), {{c1::urticaria}} (hives), {{c2::pruritus}} (itching), mild swelling.

Signs of anaphylaxis: {{c1::angioedema}} (severe swelling), difficulty breathing, wheezing, low BP, weak pulse, dizziness, GI upset, possible loss of consciousness; untreated it can lead to {{c2::cardiac arrest}}.
Mild allergic reaction: keep the patient {{c1::supine}}, give {{c2::diphenhydramine (Benadryl)}} orally, give oxygen if short of breath, and monitor vitals.
Oral diphenhydramine dose: adults {{c1::25–50 mg}}; children {{c2::1–2 mg/kg}}.
Anaphylaxis: administer epinephrine {{c1::1:1,000}} by the {{c2::IM or SC}} route.
Anaphylaxis epinephrine dose: adults {{c1::0.2–0.5 mL (0.2–0.5 mg)}}; children {{c2::0.01 mg/kg}}.
Repeat epinephrine every {{c1::10–15 minutes}} if symptoms persist, up to {{c2::3}} total doses.
Anaphylaxis: call 911 immediately after the {{c1::first epinephrine dose}}; give oxygen, monitor vitals continuously, and be ready for CPR.

Anaphylaxis mechanism: widespread {{c1::vasodilation}} drops BP (poor oxygen to the brain); {{c2::bronchoconstriction}} narrows the airway (wheezing); {{c3::histamine release from mast cells}} causes hives, itching, swelling and GI symptoms.

Epinephrine constricts blood vessels via {{c1::alpha}} receptors (raises BP), relaxes airway muscles via {{c2::beta-2}} receptors, and increases heart rate and cardiac output via {{c3::beta-1}} receptors.
Epinephrine also slows further histamine release from {{c1::mast cells and basophils}}.
Inject epinephrine (EpiPen) into the {{c1::outer thigh (vastus lateralis)}} — a large muscle with excellent blood supply for fast absorption.
An EpiPen may be injected {{c1::through clothing}}; hold it in place for {{c2::3–10 seconds}}, depending on the device instructions.
Asthma attacks are triggered by allergens, {{c1::cold air}}, {{c2::exercise}}, stress, or anxiety.
Asthma signs: coughing, wheezing, difficulty breathing, {{c1::cyanosis}} (bluish skin), chest tightness.
Asthma attack: seat the patient {{c1::upright}} and assist with their bronchodilator — usually {{c2::albuterol}}, {{c3::1–2 puffs}} as prescribed.
Asthma attack: give oxygen if short of breath or turning blue; call 911 if symptoms {{c1::do not improve within a few minutes or worsen}}; be ready for CPR.
Patients with recurring asthma should keep their bronchodilator inhaler {{c1::within reach}} during dental procedures.
Hyperventilation onset is sudden, often triggered by {{c1::anxiety}}, pain, or stress.
Hypoventilation is typically due to {{c1::respiratory depression}}, {{c2::narcotic overdose}}, or neuromuscular issues.
Hyperventilation signs: lightheadedness, rapid breathing, chest tightness, {{c1::tingling in hands/feet}}, confusion, {{c2::muscle spasms}}, dizziness.
Hypoventilation signs: slow or shallow breathing, {{c1::cyanosis}}, confusion, drowsiness, potential {{c2::respiratory arrest}}.
Hyperventilation leads to respiratory {{c1::alkalosis}} (high pH from low CO₂); hypoventilation leads to respiratory {{c2::acidosis}} and hypoxia.
Hyperventilation: seat the patient {{c1::upright}} to improve diaphragm function, and do NOT give {{c2::oxygen}}.

Slow-breathing techniques for hyperventilation: breathe through {{c1::pursed lips}} (like blowing out a candle), {{c2::cup hands}} over nose and mouth, belly (diaphragmatic) breathing, alternate nostril breathing, inhale–hold briefly–exhale slowly.

Hypoventilation is a medical emergency: call 911 immediately, place the patient {{c1::semi-reclined or supine}}, give {{c2::oxygen immediately}}, monitor vitals, and be ready for rescue breathing or CPR.
Angina: chest pressure or tightness, possibly radiating to the jaw, arm, shoulder, or back; lasts less than {{c1::10 minutes}} and is {{c2::predictable}}.
MI pain is like angina but more intense, lasts {{c1::longer than 10 minutes}}, and may include nausea, vomiting, pale or gray skin, sweating.
Suspected MI: call 911 {{c1::immediately}} — do not wait for a second nitroglycerin dose.
Chest pain: give nitroglycerin {{c1::0.4 mg}} {{c2::under the tongue}} if systolic BP is ≥{{c3::90}} mmHg.
Nitroglycerin for angina may be repeated every {{c1::5 minutes}}, to a maximum of {{c2::3 doses in 15 minutes}}.
Angina: stop treatment and keep the patient {{c1::seated upright or semi-reclined}}. MI: upright if conscious; {{c2::supine with legs elevated}} if unconscious or hypotensive.
Give oxygen at {{c1::4–6 L/min}} during angina or MI (if available / short of breath, cyanosis, or shock signs).
Suspected MI: give {{c1::325 mg chewable aspirin}} if the patient is alert and not allergic; aspirin prevents additional clot formation by inhibiting {{c2::platelet aggregation}}.
Nitroglycerin {{c1::dilates the coronary arteries}}, increasing oxygen delivery and reducing the heart's workload.
Sublingual nitroglycerin acts within {{c1::1–3 minutes}} because the tissue is highly vascular; if swallowed it is destroyed by the liver ({{c2::first-pass metabolism}}).
Cardiac arrest is often caused by a severe {{c1::heart attack}}, {{c2::electrical problems in the heart}}, trauma, overdose, or lack of oxygen.
Cardiac arrest signs: unresponsive, not breathing or only {{c1::gasping}}, and no pulse.
Cardiac arrest protocol: call 911 immediately, then begin {{c1::chest compressions}} (100–120/min, at least 2 inches deep in adults), allowing full recoil and minimizing interruptions.

basic.back: Slow respiratory rate, below the normal rate
Rapid respiratory rate, above the normal rate
Slow heart rate, below the normal rate
Fast heart rate, above the normal rate
The force against the walls of the blood vessels during contraction and relaxation of the heart
A drop in blood pressure when standing from a seated or lying position; blood pools in the legs, reducing brain perfusion
basic.extra: Did you know: it affects 1 in 5 older adults and is a common cause of fainting in the dental chair.

basic.back: A temporary rise in BP (by 10–20 mmHg) caused by stress in dental/medical settings
Temporary loss of consciousness due to reduced blood flow and oxygen to the brain (fainting)
Sudden, uncontrolled electrical activity in the brain that may cause convulsions or altered awareness

basic.front: How do ammonia capsules (smelling salts) help reverse fainting?
basic.back: They irritate the nasal membranes and stimulate the trigeminal nerve; the strong smell triggers an involuntary inhalation reflex, raising heart rate, blood pressure and breathing.

basic.front: Why does elevating the legs help a fainting (syncope) patient?
basic.back: Gravity pulls blood back toward the heart and brain, boosting brain circulation — this can reverse symptoms in minutes, sometimes faster than oxygen alone.
Sudden loss of brain function due to a blocked or burst blood vessel in the brain
A severe, life-threatening allergic reaction affecting multiple body systems, often leading to airway constriction and shock
A sudden episode of airway narrowing and mucus production causing breathing difficulty, wheezing and chest tightness
Breathing too rapidly or deeply, causing excessive elimination of CO₂
Breathing too slowly or shallowly, causing inadequate oxygen intake and CO₂ buildup

basic.front: Why can hyperventilation lead to fainting?
basic.back: Low CO₂ (respiratory alkalosis) reduces blood flow to the brain.

basic.front: What is the goal of treatment during a hyperventilation episode?
basic.back: Increase CO₂ levels in the body and slow down the breathing rate.
Temporary chest pain due to partial blockage of a coronary artery; blood flow is reduced but not completely stopped
Complete blockage of a coronary artery causing permanent death of heart muscle

basic.front: In the dental chair, how do you tell angina from a heart attack?
basic.back: You can't by the pain pattern (identical). The difference is how long the pain lasts and whether it responds to nitroglycerin: if chest pain doesn't go away after 1 dose of nitro, call 911 and treat it as a heart attack.

basic.front: Why is aspirin NOT given for angina?
basic.back: Angina is caused by temporary narrowing of the arteries, not a clot, so aspirin won't help — and if the real cause is a bleeding emergency (e.g. hemorrhagic stroke) it could make things much worse. Give aspirin only when a heart attack is suspected (benefit outweighs risk).

mcq.question: Two dental hygienists perform CPR on an unresponsive 6-year-old with no pulse. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
mcq.explanation: Children and infants get 15:2 when there are 2 rescuers (30:2 with one rescuer). 30:2 is the adult ratio for 1 or 2 rescuers.

mcq.question: Your patient collapses in the chair. She is unresponsive and not breathing, but you feel a strong carotid pulse. After calling for help, what should you do?
options: A. Begin chest compressions at 30:2
B. Give 1 rescue breath every 5–6 seconds and recheck the pulse every 2 minutes
C. Place her in the recovery position and wait for EMS
D. Attach the AED and deliver a shock
mcq.answer: B. Give 1 rescue breath every 5–6 seconds and recheck the pulse every 2 minutes
mcq.explanation: A pulse with no normal breathing calls for rescue breathing only (adult: 1 breath every 5–6 s), reassessing the pulse every 2 minutes. Compressions start only when there is no pulse; the recovery position is for a patient who is breathing.

mcq.question: Which resting respiratory rate in an adult patient is abnormal?
options: A. 12 breaths/min
B. 16 breaths/min
C. 20 breaths/min
D. 26 breaths/min
mcq.explanation: Normal adult respiration is 12–20 breaths/min; 26 is tachypnea. 12 and 20 are the edges of the normal range, not outside it.

mcq.question: A patient takes an antihypertensive every morning with breakfast. To lower her risk of orthostatic hypotension, when is the best appointment time?
options: A. Before she takes her medication
B. 30–60 minutes after her medication and meal
C. Immediately after taking the medication on an empty stomach
D. Timing makes no difference if she stands slowly
mcq.answer: B. 30–60 minutes after her medication and meal
mcq.explanation: The book advises scheduling 30–60 minutes after meds and meals. Skipping the medication instead would leave her BP uncontrolled.

mcq.question: A patient begins a generalized seizure in the dental chair. Which action is appropriate?
options: A. Place a bite block between the teeth to protect the tongue
B. Hold the arms down to prevent injury
C. Move the instruments and tray away and cushion the head
D. Break an ammonia capsule under the nose
mcq.answer: C. Move the instruments and tray away and cushion the head
mcq.explanation: Protect from injury by clearing surroundings and cushioning the head. Never restrain or place anything in the mouth. Ammonia capsules are for delayed recovery from syncope.

mcq.question: During a recall visit, a 68-year-old patient with hypertension suddenly has a drooping right side of the face and slurred speech. After calling 911, what should the hygienist do?
options: A. Give 325 mg chewable aspirin
B. Give 0.4 mg nitroglycerin sublingually
C. Note the time symptoms began and give nothing by mouth
D. Have the patient drink water and rest 15 minutes
mcq.answer: C. Note the time symptoms began and give nothing by mouth
mcq.explanation: Stroke treatment is time-sensitive, so record onset time; nothing by mouth. Aspirin (the tempting distractor) can be dangerous if the stroke is hemorrhagic — aspirin is for a suspected MI.

mcq.question: Minutes after a latex glove touches her lips, an adult patient develops wheezing, facial swelling and a weak, rapid pulse. What is the first drug to give?
options: A. Diphenhydramine 25–50 mg orally
B. Epinephrine 1:1,000, 0.3 mg IM in the outer thigh
C. Albuterol, 2 puffs
D. Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingually
mcq.answer: B. Epinephrine 1:1,000, 0.3 mg IM in the outer thigh
mcq.explanation: Rapid onset with airway and circulatory signs = anaphylaxis: epinephrine 1:1,000 IM (0.2–0.5 mg adult), then call 911. Oral diphenhydramine is for a mild, localized reaction.

mcq.question: An anxious patient breathes rapidly before an extraction and reports tingling fingers and lightheadedness. What is the best management?
options: A. Give 100% oxygen by mask
B. Seat upright and coach slow breathing, e.g. through pursed lips
C. Place supine and call 911
D. Give albuterol 2 puffs
mcq.answer: B. Seat upright and coach slow breathing, e.g. through pursed lips
mcq.explanation: This is hyperventilation (anxiety, tingling, respiratory alkalosis). The goal is to raise CO₂ — slow, controlled breathing; oxygen is NOT given. Oxygen and 911 are for hypoventilation.

mcq.question: A patient with stable angina reports chest pressure. Her BP is 84/56 mmHg. Which action is correct?
options: A. Give nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL now
B. Withhold nitroglycerin because systolic BP is below 90 mmHg
C. Give chewable aspirin 325 mg
D. Give a second nitroglycerin dose immediately
mcq.answer: B. Withhold nitroglycerin because systolic BP is below 90 mmHg
mcq.explanation: Nitroglycerin is given only if systolic BP ≥90 mmHg (it dilates vessels and would drop BP further). Aspirin is not given for angina.

mcq.question: A patient's chest pain is unrelieved 5 minutes after one 0.4 mg nitroglycerin tablet. What should the hygienist do next?
options: A. Wait another 10 minutes before acting
B. Call 911 and treat it as a heart attack
C. Dismiss the patient to see a physician today
D. Give diphenhydramine
mcq.answer: B. Call 911 and treat it as a heart attack
mcq.explanation: Angina and MI feel identical; pain that persists after 1 dose of nitro is treated as an MI — call 911 immediately.
